text: The registry rows, the workbook object, the load, the four-eyes approval, the promotion at 00:01 and the one-call rollback belong to P7 rwb-decision (ASM-A6-tables-3); rwb-case holds only an evaluated copy of an approved package version, pins the rule ID and the package version label on each decision record and on recovery_case.rule_version, and reads no rule table. Every legacy criterion that names rule_package_version, the Blob object or the effective-date job is therefore proved against the rwb-decision contract mock in this key and against the real service in RWB-ITG-E1073-ITG.
why: The legacy story and TSD P3 v3 declare the registry inside the case module while Architecture v5, the design, the ownership ruling and D-RCV-60 put it in rwb-decision, and the fifteen legacy criteria cannot be tested without one reading of who owns which artefact.

text: The seven consumed operations are served by rwb-decision on /api/recovery/decision/v1 at the legacy paths re-based there: POST and GET /admin/rule-packages/{packageCode}/versions, POST /admin/rule-package-versions/{versionId}/approve, POST /admin/rule-package-versions/{versionId}/rollback, GET /admin/rule-package-versions/{versionId}/dry-run, GET /rule-models/{packageCode}/{version} and GET /rule-catalog/{ruleId}?packageVersion=. The five authoring operations keep the legacy request and answer shapes, the model resource carries packageCode, versionLabel, checksum, model content, compiler version and valid-from date, and the catalog resource carries ruleId, packageVersion, drools_rule_name, action_text, owner_role, timer_spec, target_queue_code and outputs.
why: The Ownership Map has no row for any of the seven operations and only Architecture v5 slide 14 names the two reads, so the contract, the client and the fakes need one agreed path set and one element list on Day 1.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 14; legacy RWB-E1-073 section 12; TSD P3 v3 T2.2; Template and Rules R5.5 DP-11 and DP-13

impact: A different path or element name changes one consumed row, one client adapter and one fake; no schema, event or workflow change.

text: The pod of rwb-case is sized to hold the KieBase cache of at most 20 package versions plus the working set of the service, the heap request, the heap limit and the cache bound are reviewed values per environment, and the compiled model is held in memory only so nothing on a local volume survives a restart. The figures are provisional until the load test of the deployment story and stay out of code and out of a chart constant.
why: No source gives a memory figure or a storage statement, and the deployment cannot ship without one; the load test is the only evidence the values can rest on.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-073 preconditions and section 13; Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 27; Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1 slide 16
confirm: SCB IT infrastructure with the rwb-case owner team at the load test, and the platform observability owner for the memory view.
impact: A sizing change is a values-file change and one load-test rerun; the cache rule and the activity contract do not change.

text: The operational values of the deployment are provisional until SIT and UAT: a pod is ready only when a version is in force for every package code it serves, the readiness and liveness probes read that element with reviewed timings, the certificate subject follows the platform convention for the service, the path to rwb-decision uses the reviewed port of the platform mesh with a 2 s budget, and the image-scan gate blocks a release on a critical finding in the base image or in a KIE library with the platform patch cadence.
why: No source gives a readiness gate, a probe timing, a port, a certificate subject or a scan window, and the deployment cannot be released without them, so each is carried as a reviewed value under one assumption.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-073 preconditions; Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 11, 20 and 27; TSD P3 Case and workflow v3 T2.5; Template and Rules R7.2 s17
confirm: SCB IT infrastructure with the platform administrator and Security at SIT, and the platform observability owner for the probe definition.
impact: A threshold, a timing or a port change is a values-file change and one runbook line; no code, contract or schema change.

text: The treatment record, its terms and its approval are S2 rwb-treatment's in schema rwb_treatment and are never written in rwb_case; rwb-case consumes rwb.treatment.TreatmentApproved.v1 and rwb.payment.PaymentMissed.v1 through its case router and holds the case route state PLAN_RUNNING and PLAN_CURE_PERIOD, the plan-timer projection row in rwb_case.timer and the durable Temporal timer inside CaseWorkflow, with the treatment read through GET /api/recovery/treatment/v1/treatments/{treatmentId}; the event catalogue's consumer list for TreatmentApproved is read as not exhaustive and rwb-case is added to it.
why: The Ownership Map moves the treatment to S2 and keeps only the timer projection with P3, the Temporal design puts the restructure stage in TreatmentWorkflow, and the event catalogue lists rwb-comms and rwb-payment but not rwb-case as consumers of TreatmentApproved, so the seam the legacy story held in one service needs one stated reader and one stated writer.

text: The plan timers of GET /api/recovery/case/v1/cases/{caseId}/timers carry treatmentId, timerType INSTALLMENT_DUE or CURE_PERIOD, startedAt, expiresAt, warnAt, paused and status, every one of them optional within major version 1, with expiresAt as an offset date-time in the Asia/Bangkok zone and the array ordered by expiresAt ascending; no rule ID and no package version is returned in the timers answer, and they are read from the decision log instead.

text: The operational values are provisional until UAT: the projection lag alerts above 5 minutes, a subscription lag alerts above 500 events or 10 minutes of consumer lag, the .dlt count alerts on any event, the exception-queue count of refused plan steps alerts above 10 open cases, and the DP04 treatment product alerts when its last loaded business date is more than one day behind.
why: No source gives a threshold, a window or a band, and the deployment cannot ship without an alert value; every value stays a values-file entry and never a code constant or a business parameter.

why: The legacy story fixes one cap per queue and the target model carries both a queue cap and a personal capacity, so the answer needs one rule to be testable and two readers must not compute atCap differently.

why: The legacy screen must equal the case list count at the moment it is read, which a snapshot published on a schedule cannot guarantee, and the target table names different measures than the legacy answer, so one of the two must be declared the source.

text: A selection is answered per case: the caller sends one POST /cases/{caseId}/transfer per selected case and assembles a TransferSelection element with an ordered results array (caseId, the assignment or the refusal messageId) and the done and total counts, in the caller's order, with the summary derived from the array and no second call.
why: The legacy screen sends one request per case and the legacy criterion fixes the outcome and the summary text but no source types the element, so the contract has to fix one shape or every consumer guesses.
read: Legacy story RWB E2 012 v2 sections 4, 13 and 16; FSD P3 A2.40.4.3 AC-EXC-P3-040-04; TSD P3 API-P3-006

text: A refusal answers one element with the message ID, a reason code, the owner list with an open-case count and a cap each, or the current and target state, and the cap and the hold are read inside the operation before the first write, so a refused move changes nothing.
why: The criterion fixes what the user must see and no source types the answer; the cap and hold are columns of two tables and a read inside the operation is the only way to refuse before a write without a second call.

why: The deployment must carry a value for each of them and no source gives one; the retry policy and the 2 s user budget are the only fixed numbers.
